title: Caching Strategies
summary: Make reads faster without surprising users: decide who owns cached data, how writes update it and how long stale answers are acceptable.
body:
A cache earns its place when people ask for the same answer repeatedly and stale or missing data has an acceptable fallback. Start with the read/write ratio, freshness needs and source of truth. Redis is a common shared cache; a CDN brings public HTTP responses closer to users.

## Pick a read and write path

| Policy | On read | On write | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cache-aside | Miss loads database, then populates cache | Write database; invalidate cache | Simple, but misses and races need handling |
| Write-through | Read cached value when present | Synchronously write database and cache | Higher write latency; cache stays current on successful coordinated writes |
| Write-behind | Read cached value | Queue or buffer write, flush to database later | Fast writes, but an unflushed crash can lose data |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant C as Redis
    participant DB as Database
    App->>C: GET product:42
    C-->>App: miss
    App->>DB: SELECT product 42
    DB-->>App: row
    App->>C: SET product:42 with 60 s TTL
    Note over App,DB: Later, a write
    App->>DB: UPDATE product 42 and COMMIT
    App->>C: DEL product:42
```

With cache-aside, the application owns both paths. A miss loads the database and fills the cache. A write commits to the database first, then deletes the key so the next read reloads it. Deleting rather than overwriting avoids caching a value from a transaction that might roll back and keeps refill logic in one place. Concurrent readers can still race with that delete, as the next section shows.

Write-through does not make two systems one transaction: partial failure still needs an ordering and recovery policy. Write-behind needs a durable log or replay mechanism if acknowledged writes must survive a crash. For money transfers, commit a durable database transaction and invalidate the cache; do not treat Redis as the ledger.

## Invalidation is an ownership question

A 60-second TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of its source data or how quickly a change appears. It is an approximate staleness backstop when fills use current data. Deleting on writes reduces the stale window; change events or pub/sub can spread invalidations to many caches, and versioned keys can make old entries unreachable. But a reader can fetch an old value during a write and refill the cache after invalidation. Version checks, ordered events or a second invalidation help, with different guarantees.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Reader
    participant C as Cache
    participant DB as Database
    participant W as Writer
    R->>C: GET k
    C-->>R: miss
    R->>DB: SELECT k
    DB-->>R: old value v1
    W->>DB: UPDATE k to v2 and COMMIT
    W->>C: DEL k
    R->>C: SET k = v1
    Note over C: Stale v1 stays until the TTL expires
```

The reader fetched v1 before the write but cached it after the delete, giving an old value a fresh TTL. The window can be small, but it is real. A version check works only if invalidation preserves enough version information to reject stale fills; a lease issued on miss and invalidated by the delete can reject them too. A delayed second delete reduces the risk but cannot guarantee correctness if a reader pauses beyond the delay.

"Cache invalidation is hard" often means nobody owns every mutation path. Name each key's owner, list its writers and decide which fields may be stale before choosing the TTL. With little reuse or strict immediate consistency, skipping the cache can be the right call.

## Misses can overload the source

When a hot key expires, 1,000 simultaneous requests can all hit the database. Cache-aside does not prevent this stampede. Coalesce regeneration with single-flight or a per-key mutex; serve stale data while revalidating when allowed; jitter TTLs to avoid mass expiry.

Missing keys need protection too. Attackers can query endless nonexistent IDs and bypass the cache. Validate inputs, rate-limit and briefly negative-cache confirmed misses. A Bloom filter helps when the valid key set is known, but false positives still reach storage. Include user or tenant scope in the key before caching an authorization-sensitive 404 across requests.

## How to answer this in an interview

> At 2,000 reads and 20 writes per second for product details, I would use Redis cache-aside with a 60-second jittered TTL, invalidate the product key after a committed database write, and single-flight regeneration for hot keys. If prices must update instantly, I would bypass or version that cache rather than promise the TTL makes it current.

## Further reading

- [Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala) describes leases that prevent stale sets and thundering herds.
- [AWS: Caching best practices](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/) compares cache-aside, write-through and TTL strategies.
keyTakeaways: Cache-aside, write-through and write-behind differ in latency, failure modes and durability.
A TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not its source data's age; every mutation path needs an invalidation owner.
Single-flight or stale-while-revalidate prevents hot-key stampedes; negative caching protects against repeated misses.
Do not cache data whose consistency requirement exceeds your invalidation guarantees.
